summary: The article argues that aging utility infrastructure in US cities is directly tied to a pattern of power, internet, and water outages since September 2023. It describes cascading failures, economic and social costs, and obstacles to upgrades such as cost, logistics, and public pushback. It closes by pointing to new materials and smart sensors as a way forward and calls for funding and united public-private action.
one_line: Aging US utility infrastructure drives recurring power, water, and internet outages with large economic and social costs, though new technologies and funding could help.
key_facts: Outages across major US cities since September 2023 are linked in the article to aging utility infrastructure.
Civil engineer Daniel Martins of the University of Michigan says much of America's infrastructure was built in the post-war boom and is at the 'twilight of its intended lifespan.'
The American Society of Civil Engineers (ASCE) reports the average age of the nation's over 90,000 dams is 56 years.
Many urban water and sewer systems were installed over a century ago.
A burst water main in Atlanta on October 15, 2023 caused flooding and water disruptions, plus power outages (electrical systems were compromised to prevent electrocutions) and internet outages.
Atlanta business owner Jennifer O'Connell said the outage meant losing perishable goods to the power cut and losing the ability to conduct business online, calling it 'a double blow.'
The Anderson Economic Group estimated the internet outage on November 10, 2023 in Chicago might have cost local businesses upwards of $75 million.
Economist Laura Peterson says outages disrupt financial markets and supply chains and can weaken national economic stability.
Los Angeles city planner Mark Thompson says the challenge is not only funding but the logistics of tearing up roads and rerouting traffic to replace buried pipes and cables.
Investments in upgrades have been sluggish, with political and public pushback on upfront costs and inconveniences.
Sensors that detect early wear and tear can enable timely maintenance that prevents catastrophic failures.
Dr. Emily Sanders, a materials scientist at Stanford University, cites self-healing concrete and corrosion-resistant alloys as materials that can greatly extend infrastructure longevity.
Outages endanger vulnerable people such as the elderly and those with medical dependence on electricity, and school closures from water main breaks or lack of internet deprive children of education.
